📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

According to recent reports, peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps.

In a recent development, following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm.

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”.

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

Sources indicate that “Availability,” he mentioned, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and remarked he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel mentioned. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”.

Industry observers note that asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”.

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

It has been revealed that but on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”.

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone demonstrated he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

It has been revealed that shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

It has been revealed that england played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

Recent findings suggest that in the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Things could’ve been much different for Paolo Maldini at AC Milan without two major figures in his life and career.

In a recent development, maldini has two faces at Milan, but both remain adored by the fanbase. Firstly, you have the legendary defender, whose number was retired with him, a sign of respect and a chance to honour a career and legacy which surpasses many in the game.

Then, he returned as the sporting director, ending the Scudetto drought. Of course, that story didn’t have an ending as romantic as his playing career, but his legacy lives on. In fact, he may be voted into the Hall of Fame in the very near future.

Speaking to Tuttomercatoweb, via PianetaMilan, Maldini looked at the earliest stages of his career, as well as when he really took off for the Rossoneri.

“When my father took me to try out for AC Milan, I liked playing goalkeeper, but luckily I ended up choosing to be a defender. I played football with my friends in the park and at the youth club: I didn’t feel like I was destined for success at all, and until the day I made my debut, I never thought I could reach the highest levels.

“My dad always told me that the most important thing is to have fun, because if you treat it only as a job, it loses its magic.”.

According to recent reports, “There’s one person in particular who believed in me and wanted me to play when I was 15: Nils Liedholm, then AC Milan’s coach. He loved showing his faith in young players, and once, during a break, he asked me whether I preferred to play on the right or left. I replied that it was obviously his choice, but it was a gesture that helped me a lot.”.

It has been revealed that as they say, one change and the rest is history. With Maldini, that was certainly the case.

Published: 07:00 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 16:17 EST, 13 November 2026.

It was gone 11pm when Thomas Tuchel was shaking the hands of Harry Kane’s parents on the Wembley pitch while the children of England’s record appearance maker enjoyed the run of the national stadium in front of 90,000 empty seats.

This was time for Kane to fully take in the emotion of an historic night alongside his family and that Tuchel was out there too felt instructive of their relationship.

Kane and Tuchel had frank conversations last month about the World Cup fallout, on how England might be best tinkering with their selection when chasing games.

The manager respects and values his captain’s opinion on these things, recognising that he is almost completely agenda-free, as they attempt to better plot a route to silverware in readiness for the European Championship in 18 months’ time.

If there was uncertainty about identity and style when the World Cup crunch arrived, when Enzo Fernandez was pulling stupid faces and the colour drained from England faces, then players have felt that the detail on how Tuchel wants to move forward has been clear across the first two camps since America.

Thursday night was not vintage against a Croatia team they battered 7-0 a few weeks back. Tuchel and Kane both admitted that afterwards but it is noticeable that there is a defined proposal on how they intend to attack in a slightly different way.

Thomas Tuchel embraces Harry Kane's wife Katie at Wembley on Thursday night.

Harry Kane (centre) and Co are changing the way they attack after the World Cup.

According to recent reports, were Tuchel to have been able to pick a first-choice back four then the win would likely have been more comfortable, Croatia benefiting from individual errors. And a lack of cutting edge inside the box hindered the hosts too.

The idea behind what they were doing appeared well thought out though and that should bring about some gentle encouragement.

The full backs, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Lewis Hall, were both consistently worked into hugely dangerous areas in the inside channels, while the make-up of Tuchel’s midfield felt very deliberate as well.

It is no coincidence that England enjoyed the highest amount of possession in the half spaces ten yards inside Croatia’s half. That is a clear directive, with both Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice drifting wider to create overloads and the full backs pushed into threatening spaces.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Declan understands the game like he’s almost a coach on the field and in a perfect position to manage all these things from behind,’ Tuchel noted this week. To have a constant interchanging unit, he does need brains.

These are the rotations that the Three Lions didn’t engineer enough of over in the United States, with Kane dropping deep as he does and completing that wonder crossfield pass for the Morgan Rogers opener.

They are the moments that Tuchel is preaching, Jude Bellingham taking up an unusual position in order to stretch Croatia as he squared for the Chelsea forward.

What Tuchel needs now is to work on how that can be translated into making sure his very best players can affect matches more regularly inside the opponent’s box.

Jude Bellingham only touched the ball four times in Croatia's box in the 2-1 win.

England manager Thomas Tuchel will speak to his players about what to do if racial abuse mars Sunday’s Nations League group decider against Spain in Madrid.

The England team have been on the wrong end of racism in Madrid before – back in 2004 – and refused to play a friendly there in 2008, insisting the fixture be moved to Seville.

In March this year, meanwhile, Spanish fans chanted anti-Muslim songs during a game with Egypt in Barcelona and the World champions have been subsequently ordered by FIFA to play their next friendly in a partially-closed stadium.

There will be a full house at Athletico Madrid’s Riyadh Air Metropolitano stadium as England try to topple Spain from the top of their group on Sunday and Tuchel said: ‘I think I hear about it [the Barcelona incident] for the first time that this happens. I think it's unacceptable.

‘In any stadium we will never accept racism.

‘I expect full support from the Spanish crowd for the Spanish team. But we will not expect anything else. And I think the referee in the games and the officials know about that.

‘I think we had a same discussion before the Serbia game [last year]. There is a protocol in place.

‘Yeah, maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Spain].’.

Tuchel and the FA expect a hostile atmosphere in Madrid, especially as two Real players – Jude Bellingham and Trent Alexander-Arnold - will be in the England squad.

Last year’s Serbia game passed without incident in Belgrade and the FA are confident the same will apply this weekend.

It has been revealed that seven years ago in Sofia, though, captain Harry Kane almost led the England team off the field after following FIFA protocols by alerting the referee to abuse aimed at Tyrone Mings, Raheem Sterling and Marcus Rashford. The game was paused while the culprits were thrown out.

‘I still think the protocol is in place and it's important that the players know about is,’ added Tuchel.

‘And then yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. The best answers are on the pitch.’.

The FIFA protocol – adopted by UEFA and the Premier League – is a four step-process that starts with a player alerting match officials and is followed by a warning to the crowd, a possible suspension of play and, if necessary, the abandonment of the game.

That Kane only touched it six times inside the 18-yard area and Bellingham on just four occasions points to a team still figuring themselves out.

Industry observers note that that will be put to the severe test in Madrid on Sunday. England do not beat the truly elite nations; never have.

And it’ll be interesting to see whether Tuchel sticks to this sort of plan, one designed to dominate, or if he instead relies on the counter-attacking ability of a group he has viewed as a ‘Premier League team’ before now, leaning into their physicality.

If England are feeling confident enough, giving this tweaked style a go against the world champions might offer them some answers on what could be achieved when the proper silverware is on the line.

Ashley Young reckons it is time for Manchester United to move on from Bruno Fernandes and feels there is a Premier League star who should be signed to replace him.

Fernandes has consistently been the Red Devils’ best player since joining from Sporting in January 2020.

However, at 32 years old and with new manager Mauricio Pochettino arriving this week, doubts over whether Fernandes will remain the focal point of the team are being raised.

The United captain is into the final few months of his contract and has reportedly rejected two offers of a fresh deal.

The club has the option to extend his current contract by another month, which would prevent Fernandes leaving on a free transfer in the summer, but he could still be sold in 2027 if that option is taken up.

Former Red Devils man Young reckons it is time to move on from Fernandes and thinks the man to replace him is Nottingham Forest and England midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White.

The former Wolves star turns 27 in January and Young feels now is the time for Manchester United to make him their main man, replacing Fernandes.

‘He’s been unbelievable for the club, the standout performer,’ Young remarked of Fernandes on Overlap Daily. ‘But there’s been so much that’s come about. He’s turned down another contract, we’re hearing.

It has been revealed that ‘You want to build around a player. He’s 33 next year. Age is nothing but a number, but he’s not in his peak. I wouldn’t say past it, but he’s getting older now.

Chelsea and Manchester United led the tributes to Juan Mata after he announced his retirement from professional football.

The former Spain international, who lifted the 2010 World Cup and 2012 European Championship, has hung up his boots at the age of 38 after leaving Australian giants Melbourne Victory in September.

Mata started his career at Real Madrid’s academy before moving to Valencia in 2007, where he won the 2008 Copa del Rey alongside fellow future World Cup winners David Silva and David Villa.

He moved to Chelsea in 2011 and helped the Blues win the Champions League and FA Cup in his first season at the club. The diminutive midfielder was crowned Chelsea’s Player of the Year in both of his two full seasons in west London before leaving for Manchester United in January 2014.

Recent findings suggest that mata helped United win the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup before his departure in 2022. He then spent the latter years of his career with Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory.

Mata declared his retirement with a 50-second video posted on his social media channels.

Industry observers note that in the video, Mata sits in a changing room, staring at a pair of football boots. He then turns around and hangs them up on a peg, with the caption: “Sometimes to love is to let go. Thanks, football.”.

A full statement was also posted on Mata’s official website, in which he admitted “Football will never leave my life” and that he would continue to use football “as a vehicle for development.”.

Mata is best known for co-founding Common Goal, a global movement in which players, coaches, and clubs pledge at least 1% of their salaries to fund grassroots football charities.

Recent findings suggest that “I was able to keep going for so many years because of the sheer joy of playing. Waking up every morning looking forward to training and playing, whether at magnificent grounds such as Old Trafford, Stamford Bridge or Mestalla.

“Or back when I was starting out at Juventud Estadio, where the pitch turned into a mud bath every winter. I believe that kind of passion is fundamental to everything in life.

According to recent reports, “Football will never leave my life. There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development. I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer.”.

Mauricio Pochettino reflected on a dream ending to his United States tenure as he prepares to take over at Manchester United.

Pochettino was appointed as Man Utd's new head coach last week, but he stayed on to oversee the USA's CONCACAF Nations League two-legged quarter-final tie with Haiti.

The USA romped to a 6-0 win on Saturday, and then followed it up with a routine 2-0 success in Cincinnati on Tuesday.

Pochettino, who took over in 2024, bows out having overseen a six-game unbeaten run since the end of the USA's World Cup campaign.

Recent findings suggest that the USA had 14 shots worth a combined 1.43 expected goals, and enjoyed 74.2% possession. Christian Pulisic scored a stunning overhead kick, while Julian Hall netted his fifth goal in the space of six caps; at 18 years and 238 days old, he is the youngest player ever to net five goals for the USMNT.

"The way we played, that is what we dreamed of when we arrived," Pochettino told reporters.

In a recent development, "When you talk about these games, it looks like it was easy. But Haiti is a World Cup team. The players make the job easier.

"We knew that we have talented players, and in the last six games, being unbeaten and playing against a tough opponent, I see the team really enjoy playing football, playing soccer.".

And Pochettino has no doubt that the future is bright for the USA, even if he will not be the coach at the helm.

In a recent development, "I am sure that this group of players, they will achieve major things in the future. I have no doubt," he mentioned.

"[Experienced] players with a mix of younger, with the talent that is coming, I think it's a perfect combination.

"The way that they are leading all the things now, I think it's about being proud of the players, the whole squad, the whole pool of players.

"Of course, it's tough because it's emotional, because I really love these guys and I love the players, I love the staff, I love you, the fans and everything.

Recent findings suggest that "And even if sometimes we have not agreed in our way to see things, that is life, to accept the critics, to accept that someone can disagree with you, with your ideas and see things in a different way. But that is life and you grow through there.".

Ivan Toney’s bid to move the date of his assault trial to avoid clashing with Euro 2028 games has been refused by a judge.

The England footballer, 30, hopes to be selected to play for the national side in the next European Championship after featuring in this summer’s World Cup .

Toney is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva during a confrontation at a nightclub in Wardour Street, central London, on December 6, 2025.

He denied assault occasioning actual bodily harm at a court hearing last month and a date for a three- to four-day trial was fixed for June 12, 2028, which is three days into the Uefa Euro 2028 tournament.

Bid to move footballer Ivan Toney’s trial date to avoid Euro 2028 clash refused.

‘Bruising’ 7.2% annual fall in inner London house prices is biggest in 17 years.

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, which Toney did not attend, his barrister Mozammel Hossain KC mentioned: “It came to our attention that… there may be potentially a football match called the European championships in 2028 between June 9 and July 9.”.

Mr Hossain proposed a trial date in August that year, adding: “We ask you please that the matter be put back to then for a trial so that if the defendant is included in this football tournament he can play.

“My knowledge of football is very limited but I am told he was included in the last one in 2024 and the England squad for the World Cup.”.

Judge Tony Baumgartner called it a “speculative” application.

He refused the request, saying: “It does not seem to me to be in the interest of justice to disturb the date that was already fixed.”.

The judge stated the application could be made again if Toney is selected for the England squad.

An earlier hearing was told the alleged assault happened at the 100 Wardour Street club during a confrontation between the defendant and Mr Da Silva.

It was heard the two men “squared up to each other”, before Toney allegedly “lunged forward and headbutted the complainant, followed by a few punches”.

The Metropolitan Police investigated and the footballer was charged in late July.

Toney, of Northampton, has made 10 international appearances and scored one goal.

He missed out on the latest squad for the country’s Nations League ties.

Toney started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.

He scored 72 goals during four years with the Bees before making a surprise switch in 2024 to Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli.

Manchester United have identified three potential defensive signings for Mauricio Pochettino in the January transfer window, according to reports.

Pochettino arrived at United’s training ground on Wednesday afternoon to begin his stint as head coach following the decision to sack Michael Carrick last week.

United have faced criticism over their transfer activity in the summer as they spent £155 million on signing three midfielders in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.

Pochettino now arrives at Old Trafford short of options with striker Benjamin Sesko sidelined until next year with a shin injury, while Luke Shaw has missed United’s last seven fixtures.

According to Sky Sports, United are willing to bolster Pochettino’s squad in the January window and the club will consult the Argentine over any potential signings.

The report claims that Everton centre-back Jarrad Branthwaite and Fulham’s Calvin Bassey are two players who United are considering for January.

Elsewhere, reports in Spain claim that Barcelona left-back Alejandro Balde is open to a move to United in the upcoming transfer window.

The international break has played out something like an Oprah Winfrey show for the Arsenal squad.

Oprah, back in 2004, marched around her studio, declaring all those in the audience had won a car. Just the 276 Pontiac G6s dished out, for those wondering.

Andrea Berta has seemingly been following that example at Arsenal. “You get a contract! You get a contract! You get a contract! You get a contract! Everybody gets a contract!”.

It started with the news that Declan Rice had reached an agreement over a latest long-term deal, one that will see him join Bukayo Saka on around £350,000-a-week.

It has been revealed that jurrien Timber, too, is set to commit his future to the club. Like Rice, he had entered the final two years of his current deal but the intention was always for Arsenal to tie him down beyond that.

According to recent reports, there was more. David Raya has agreed fresh terms as well and will sign a newly introduced contract, a year on from receiving a pay rise. This deal will keep him at Arsenal through to 2030.

Piero Hincapie wanted in and is understood to have joined the extension club. The defender only signed for the Gunners permanently in the summer and that deal did not expire until 2031.

However, Hincapie has been rewarded with improved terms for his contribution to the title-winning season and a 12-month extension on the previous deal.

A busy period, then, for those involved in the building and managing of this squad. An extremely indicative one, too, both of how far Arsenal have come and where they want to get to.

It was not that long ago that contract negotiations for key players were a major source of stress for the club.

Recent findings suggest that under Arsene Wenger, Alexis Sanchez made it clear he had no desire to sign a newly introduced deal. Arsenal decided not to sell and he went into the last year of his contract, before joining Manchester United in a swap deal with Henrikh Mkhitaryan.

Terrified of losing Mesut Ozil for free and having been dragged into the final six months of his deal in 2018, Arsenal threw the kitchen sink at him and gave him a £350,000-a-week deal.

For years, Arsenal fans knew exactly when the contracts of the most important players would run out, almost fearing the two years leading up to that.

Transfer news LIVE: Arsenal in Vinicius talks; Man Utd deal confirmed.

Arsenal get new Havertz penalty review as Premier League panel confirm error.

Make 2026 the year of working smarter.

Not so now. Rice has entered the final 18 months of his existing deal but there was no real sense of jeopardy. The assumption was always that an extension would be agreed and that has proved correct.

This is now a club that players want to sign but just as crucially want to stay at. Rice’s fresh deal will commit his prime years to the club, as will be the case with Raya.

According to recent reports, you get a contract! You get a contract! You get a contract! You get a contract! Everybody gets a contract!

Had Rice wished to explore his options elsewhere, he would have had his pick of the elite clubs across Europe, as would William Saliba before he signed a fresh deal last year.

Arsenal might not be able to sign the most high-profile players from clubs like Real Madrid, as the summer pursuit of Vinicius Junior showed, but they can now protect their own assets regardless of who wants them.

Industry observers note that there are still decisions to be made over other situations. Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz are both out of contract in 2028 as it stands. So too is Ben White and it is understood that as with Odegaard, no contract talks have yet taken place with the club.

Industry observers note that however, the dynamic is very different to the one Arsenal have had to put up with in the past. These are not desperate negotiations. If these are players are leave in the transfer windows ahead, it feels like that would be a club-led decision.

Sources indicate that these contract extensions also point to the power Mikel Arteta has and the priorities of the club. This is not about building a squad for five or six years down the line. Everything is centred towards giving Arteta the tools to win immediately.

That was apparent in the summer signings of Ezri Konsa and Bruno Guimaraes, both now 29, and in the handing out of huge contracts to take players well into their 30s.

Arteta has signed a contract of his own through to 2030 and it is all about maximising every opportunity for major trophies between now and then.

Industry observers note that his priority is this season and the three beyond it. What happens after that, in terms of the age profile of the squad or the contract situations in the squad, might not be Arteta’s problem.

In a recent development, by then he might be driving off into the sunset. Probably not in a Pontiac G6.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Crystal Palace are closing in on the appointment of Thomas Frank as their new head coach, according to The Athletic, with the former Tottenham Hotspur and Brentford boss expected to replace Pierre Sage at Selhurst Park.
  • It has been revealed that the 53-year-old faces an enormous challenge after Palace collected just seven points from their opening 10 Premier League matches, leaving them at the foot of the table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Blain | 16 Nov 2026 15:28.

Crystal Palace are closing in on the appointment of Thomas Frank as their new head coach, according to The Athletic, with the former Tottenham Hotspur and Brentford boss expected to replace Pierre Sage at Selhurst Park.

It has been revealed that the 53-year-old faces an enormous challenge after Palace collected just seven points from their opening 10 Premier League matches, leaving them at the foot of the table. He has only a handful of days to work with his new squad before Saturday's trip to Coventry City, making an immediate improvement essential.

Frank has plenty of rebuilding to do after his difficult spell in north London, but his successful seven-year stint at Brentford offers encouragement.

Sports Mole looks at three priorities that should dominate his in-tray in the first few months.

Sources indicate that frank's most urgent task will be to address a defence that has conceded 24 goals in just ten Premier League matches, the worst record in the division. Palace have also shipped eight goals from set pieces, including four during their current run of four consecutive defeats.

Recent findings suggest that it is a problem that predates Sage's arrival, having also troubled Oliver Glasner, but Frank has a reputation for organising competitive sides and could bring some much-needed structure. At Brentford, he alternated between a 3-5-2 and 4-3-3, with the former potentially straightforward to implement given Palace's familiarity with a back three.

However, the personnel available to him remain a concern. Palace did not adequately replace Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guehi, while summer arrivals Takehiro Tomiyasu, Axel Disasi and 18-year-old Honest Ahanor have not necessarily provided the defensive stability required.

Disasi is a particularly interesting case. The Chelsea loanee has an opportunity to establish himself as a key figure, but Frank must decide whether he is the right partner for the existing defensive options or whether further recruitment is required.

Frank's Brentford teams were also particularly dangerous from dead-ball situations, ranking among the Premier League's best for set-piece expected goals during his time there. Bringing that same attention to detail to both boxes could make an immediate difference.

According to recent reports, adam Wharton's decline in influence has been another major frustration for Palace. Only a few months ago, the midfielder was attracting reported interest from Chelsea, Manchester City and Liverpool, having established himself as one of the most exciting young English players in the Premier League.

Sources indicate that now, the noise surrounding his future has quietened considerably. Wharton missed out on England's 2026 World Cup squad and has struggled to reproduce the performances that previously made him so highly rated.

His average performance rating has dropped from fourth-best among Palace players in 2025-26 to seventh this season, with his contribution in possession and defensive work both coming under scrutiny.

Some of those difficulties appear connected to the unfamiliar responsibilities he has been given under Sage. Wharton has struggled to track runners and protect the space in front of the defence, and while not known for his attacking prowess, his influence in transition and in the final third has waned, registering fewer accurate long balls and key passes per 90 in the Premier League.

Frank must find a role that allows the 22-year-old to dictate games without leaving him exposed defensively. Restoring Wharton's confidence and getting him closer to his previous level would represent a significant boost, both for Palace's survival hopes and his longer-term development.

Palace's problems in front of goal are not quite as severe as their defensive shortcomings, but Frank will need to address the uncertainty surrounding his centre-forward options.

Sources indicate that jean-Philippe Mateta wanted to leave during the summer and is approaching the final months of his contract, while an injury has already disrupted his campaign. The Frenchman has yet to score in the Premier League this season and has accumulated more red cards than goals, leaving his future increasingly uncertain.

Jorgen Strand Larsen has also struggled to convince since arriving, managing just one goal in eight league appearances. His record of 19 goals in 79 top-flight outings hardly suggests he is ready to become a reliable long-term replacement for Mateta.

Sources indicate that frank may therefore need to look beyond Selhurst Park when the January window opens. A reunion with Richarlison, who looks to be available from ex-club Spurs, is one possibility worth considering, particularly given the Brazilian's previous experience under the Dane.

Sources indicate that palace spent heavily on 11 summer arrivals, so chairman Steve Parish may be reluctant to sanction another significant recruitment drive. Nevertheless, losing Mateta without securing a dependable replacement would leave Frank with a major problem.

With Palace already facing a fight to climb away from the bottom of the table, Frank cannot afford to wait until January to make improvements.

Defensive organisation, Wharton's revival and a reliable goalscorer represent three clear priorities if he is to turn a troubled season around.

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Jordan Pickford should still get the nod as England's number one goalkeeper over James Trafford, so says Ashley Young.

Thomas Tuchel has used this Nations League campaign to split time evenly between Pickford and Trafford.

Pickford has been England's undisputed number one since 2017, with the 32-year-old making 94 appearances and keeping 49 clean sheets.

Peter Shilton (125) is the only goalkeeper to have won more caps for England than Pickford, though he now has fierce competition from Leeds United shot-stopper Trafford, who made a string of fine saves to help the Three Lions beat Spain on Sunday.

Pickford has now not started four of England's last seven competitive internationals, having only not been in the XI for two of their previous 41 beforehand.

However, in their last nine competitive matches without Jordan Pickford, England have only kept two clean sheets and conceded an average of two goals per game (18 in total).

And even though Trafford's performance saw plenty of calls for the 24-year-old to be installed as England's first-choice goalkeeper, Young has backed his former Everton club-mate Pickford.

"You've always got to give goalkeepers the chance to show what they're about," Young said on The Overlap Daily.

"Playing as a defender, you want to know who's behind you as a goalkeeper. Right, that's it, this is who's going to be our number one. That's who’s going to be in goal. And I think, rightly so, Jordan Pickford has earned 94 caps for a reason.

It has been revealed that A POTM performance from James Trafford! https://t.co/LZY2ZZ7oSn.

— England (@England) November 16, 2026.

According to recent reports, "He has been at three World Cups, two Euros; he’s got 49 clean sheets. It's understandable, but for me, Pickford is England's number one.

"Of course, Trafford has come in and done well, made some great saves at the end of the Spain game, but I think Pickford is a goalkeeper who demonstrates himself more with his feet when playing for England, because Thomas Tuchel wants that, more passing out from the back and whatnot.

Sources indicate that "I'm more confident in Pickford than Trafford with his feet. But when you've got different managers, it's different. At Everton, they play out from the back at times but not as much as England do. For me, Pickford's England's number one.".

Trafford has impressed for Leeds this season, although he did make an error leading directly to a goal when his mistake was pounced on by Evanilson in Leeds' recent defeat to Bournemouth.

Nevertheless, Trafford has a goals prevented figure of 4.4, which is the joint-best in the Premier League, along with Brighton's Bart Verbruggen.

Trafford's 82.2% save ratio also tops the charts in the division.

Pickford, meanwhile, has registered a 73.7% save ratio, and 1.1 goals prevented.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool have received a surprise boost ahead of their Premier League showdown against Manchester United, with star striker Alexander Isak handed a rest while on international duty.

Sweden boss Graham Potter pledged to name a strong team against Poland for the Nations League B dead rubber - the Swedes already confirmed as group winners ahead of kick-off.

But despite that promise, Isak remained on the bench for the full 90 minutes on Tuesday night as Sweden secured a 1-1 draw in Poland to conclude a successful Nations League campaign.

Sweden will move up to the top tier of the Nations League for the 2028-29 edition of the competition, allowing Isak to mix with Europe’s elite on the international stage.

Isak missed three games for Sweden during the last international break after picking up a thigh issue, which then prevented the 27-year-old from featuring for Liverpool against Manchester City and LASK.

But rather than returning from international duty with an injury, this time Isak will come back to Merseyside fully rested for Sunday’s clash with Man United.

So far this season, Isak has made 14 appearances for Liverpool across all competitions, grabbing eight goals and one assist.

After an injury-frustrated debut season at Anfield - Isak suffering a fibula fracture in December - following his £130million move from Newcastle, the Swede has become a central figure to Andoni Iraola’s aims.

Aside from the two games he missed due to a thigh problem, Isak has played minutes in every fixture he has been available for.

Isak has only faced Man Utd once as a Liverpool player, taken off after 72 minutes at Anfield during a 2-1 defeat in October 2025 before missing the return fixture at Old Trafford due to an adductor matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mauricio Pochettino has arrived at Carrington as he begins life as Manchester United manager, and he has ensured that training sessions are already underway.

The Manchester Evening News reports that Pochettino’s trusted lieutenants Jesus Perez, Toni Jimenez, and his son Sebastiano Pochettino carried out training at Carrington on Wednesday morning.

Pochettino had sent the trio ahead to Manchester on Sunday, in order to ensure his tenure got off to the smoothest start possible.

Perez, Jimenez, and Pochettino Jr also oversaw training on Tuesday, with Man Utd players not called up for international duty returning from a four-day break.

During the first half of the international break, Michael Carrick led training - despite Man Utd sounded out a move for the Argentine to replace the former midfielder after a disappointing to start to the season.

Although Pochettino has visited Carrington for the first time in his role as Man Utd boss Wednesday afternoon, he will not lead training until Thursday.

The Argentine head coach signed off his stint as United States Men’s National Team [USMNT] manager with a 2-0 victory over Haiti on Tuesday evening UK time, ensuring the USA advanced to the semi-finals of the CONCACAF Nations League in March 2027.

Strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, analyst Alec Scott, and coach Miguel D’Agostino stayed with Pochettino Stateside for the Haiti game, with all three joining Pochettino’s backroom staff at Old Trafford.

D’Agostino is a former teammate of Pochettino and a long-standing member of the ex-Chelsea head coach’s inner circle, while Tuya and Scott have impressed the Argentine enough since joining his USA set-up to be taken across the pond.

Now, Pochettino’s focus turns to Liverpool - his first game in charge of Man United taking place at Anfield on Sunday afternoon.

Latest Update: SCOTLAND 2 NORTH MACEDONIA 1: John McGinn at the double to spare the blushes of Pocognoli's shaky Scots on skipper Robertson's major night

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026.
  • On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026.

On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.

Coming 40 years and a day after his friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish, pulled on a Scotland jersey for the 102nd and final time, Andy Robertson joined the great man on a mark which, for years, seemed beyond the reach of mere mortals.

According to recent reports, by time up, history had mercifully repeated itself at Hampden. Back in the day, Dalglish, by then player-manager at Anfield, sailed into the international sunset on the back of a routine 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Facing another opponent of modest ability, Robertson’s red letter day didn’t go quite as smoothly. Yet, when the Tottenham man is old and grey and reflecting on the night he created history, the annals will at least record a slender victory.

While his side did just about enough to prevail here, this was another fraught night for Sebastien Pocognoli.

You can talk about the need for patience under the fresh manager until the cows come home. But North Macedonia are 71st in FIFA’s rankings. Scotland are 43rd.

John McGinn celebrates in trademark fashion after netting Scotland's winner from the spot.

At Hampden Park, in front of an expectant crowd, Scotland should be putting them to the sword with something to spare.

Yet, for long enough, the Belgian’s newly introduced-look side were flat, predictable and plodding. It noted much that it took the intervention of VAR for them to get the penalty which would ultimately lead to three points being accrued.

John McGinn’s second half double saved the Belgian’s blushes and truthfully there was little else to get the Tartan Army off their seats.

Sources indicate that too many substantial-name players scarcely merited pass marks. Too few looked comfortable in the system the manager is trying to bed in.

If it was a step in the right direction, it was a small one. After five games under the affable Belgian, the progress has certainly not been startling.

While it goes without saying that beating the Swiss in St Gallen on Monday will be an inordinately tougher task, having some hope of moving up a place and securing a kinder draw for the Euros is still better than no hope.

Regardless of what pot they end up in when the draw is made in Belfast next month, a radical improvement will certainly be required across the board if they are to stand any chance of qualifying for the tournament via the front door.

As well as the achievements of Robertson and Dalglish, the career of Craig Gordon was acknowledged before the match with the 84-times capped keeper deservedly afforded a warm hand by the Tartan Army.

McGinn slots home his penalty after Ben Gannon-Doak had been brought down in the area.

There were absolutely no excuses for Scotland here. North Macedonia were a tier-two team in name only. They arrived at Hampden having not won in 12 matches and not scored in eight.

Another Pocognoli game saw another back-three combination. This time Luke Graham was selected in the centre of the unit with Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney deployed either side of the Stoke man in what were their first appearances under the Belgian.

Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak were tasked with providing the width in the 3-4-3. Scott McTominay slotted back into an advanced role beside John McGinn with the returning Che Adams asked to lead the line.

Recent findings suggest that for all there was a healthy crowd in excess of 40,000 inside Hampden, the atmosphere was subdued. In the four Nations League games to date under the latest manager, the side hadn’t exactly given the supporters much to feed off.

Despite some major guns returning, Scotland made a laboured start to their night’s work. It noted much that Graham, on his second appearance, was busier than any defender in white.

In a recent development, the first opening came as a result of an opposition error. John McGinn found Billy Gilmour who fed the overlapping Robertson. The skipper’s cross was well out of Adams’ reach.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his first Hampden win as Scotland boss but it was a nervy night.

Sources indicate that although Ljupche Doriev worried Angus Gunn with a curling effort, Scotland began to exert some degree of control on the match. Lewis Ferguson kept the visitors hemmed in with a header into McTominay’s feet. The Napoli man saw his shot on the spin well saved by Stole Dimitrievski.

Pocognoli was frustrated when Slovakian referee Michal Ocenas blew for a foul on McTominay, his justifiable gripe being that playing an advantage would have seen Robertson have a crack at goal.

Dimitrievski had a decent night. Although Adams’ flashing header from McGinn’s corner took a deflection, a reflex save at his near post added to Scotland’s frustration.

According to recent reports, north Macedonia were a spirited but ordinary side. They still had enough to thwart Pocognoli’s men.

Recent findings suggest that gannon-Doak saw plenty of the ball down the right, yet the end product often wasn’t there. The Bournemouth man did tee up Billy Gilmour for one dangerous cross. McTominay tried to replicate his iconic overhead kick against Denmark nearly a year ago. This time, his aim wasn’t true.

You could hardly blame Pocognoli’s star man for failing to find the net on that occasion.

Scott McTominay attempts an overhead spectacular a year on from THAT goal at Hampden.

Industry observers note that that wasn’t the case a few moments later when Adams slipped him in. Dimitrievski saved McTominay’s strike with an outstretched leg when he should have been picking the ball out of his net.

Adams had just blazed a strike high over the top while one-on-one with the keeper although the offside flag saved his blushes.

The visitors came closer to edging ahead when Eljif Elmas played the pass of the match over Scotland’s static defence to pick out Ezgjan Alioski. His lay-off was smashed into the side net by Enis Bardhi.

A wholly uninspiring first-half concluded with Robertson advancing up the left and launching a cross halfway to Castlemilk. This was not going well.

Pocognoli waited on the edge of the pitch for his players returning, his enthusiastic applause clearly audible in the arena.

His hopes of a breakthrough at the outset of the second period were dashed in extraordinary fashion. Adams did well to chase a ball down to the line and cut it back. McTominay and his marker couldn’t connect, leaving Gilmour the simple task of firing into an unguarded net. Leaning back, his failure to even hit the target was unfathomable.

Elmin Rastoder celebrates after silencing Hampden with a leveller for North Macedonia.

Within seconds, the sense of relief inside Hampden was palpable as the opener finally arrived. Porteous got enough distance on his clearing header for Adams to barge Visar Musliu out of the way.

Recent findings suggest that mcGinn was alert to the situation and burst into the box. His crisp strike finally had the beating of the goalkeeper.

It should have settled Pocognoli’s side and paved the way for a comfortable result. Instead, they were pegged back within three minutes.

Recent findings suggest that it was all just so simple and so avoidable. Bardhi’s whipped corner only needed McTominay to outjump his man. Flat-footed as the delivery arrived, he could only watch on in horror as Elmin Rastoder’s flashing header beat Angus Gunn.

Although Gilmour worked the keeper with a low strike, North Macedonia also sniffed a second goal. Time and time again, they got into pockets of space on the flanks and fired in dangerous crosses.

Adams made way for Oli McBurnie, the Hull man desperately hoping for his first goal on his 21st international appearance. He had a gilt-edged chance to get off the mark when rolled in by McGinn, but selflessly passed to the overlapping Gannon-Doak.

Scotland move on to their final game away in Switzerland as they look to finish on a high note.

Industry observers note that the winger appeared to take a heavy touch which allowed the keeper to rescue the situation. VAR, however, spotted that Dimitrievski had impeded him. Penalty.

McGinn did the necessary from 12 yards, smashing the ball straight down the middle for his 24th international goal.

North Macedonia, to their credit, kept going for it. They sensed a fragility in Scotland. Everyone in the ground could.

In a recent development, mcGinn’s calm conversion proved to be just about enough to get the job done. But it’s fair to suggest that we are still awaiting lift-off in the fresh era.

It has been revealed that SCOTLAND (3-4-1-2): Gunn; Porteous, Graham, Tierney; Gannon-Doak (Hickey 76), Ferguson, Gilmour (Christie 76), Robertson; McGinn; Adams (McBurnie 67), McTominay. Booked: Ferguson. Manager: Sebastien Pocognoli.

NORTH MACEDONIA (4-2-3-1): Dimitrievski; Ilievski, Mladenovski, Musliu, Alioski; Gashtarov (Elezi 64), Elmas (Stankovski 78); Churlinov (Maleski 64), Bardhi, Doriev (Nikolov 85); Rastoder. Booked: None. Manager: Goce Sedloski.

Referee: Michal Ocenas (Slovakia).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 16 Nov 2026 15:36, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 15:38.

Como head coach Cesc Fabregas was reportedly discussed by Manchester United chiefs as a potential replacement for Michael Carrick.

Fabregas is regarded as one of the brightest young coaches in world football, with the 39-year-old hugely impressive since taking charge of Como.

The former midfielder has won 46, drawn 26 and lost 26 of his 98 matches in charge of Como since being appointed permanent head coach in July 2024.

The Italian club's fourth-placed finish in the 2025-26 Serie A campaign saw them qualify for this season's Champions League, and they have impressed in the competition this term, including a standout 9-1 victory over Lille last time out.

Como are currently fourth in the Serie A table, only six points behind the leaders Lazio, and the team's style of football under Fabregas has been excelllent.

Man United lost 4-1 to Como in the Champions League earlier this season, and it appears only a matter of time before Fabregas makes the move to a major club.

According to The Athletic, Fabregas' name was mentioned when Man United had an executive committee meeting on November 5.

The report claims that Man United CEO Omar Berrada is a huge fan of Fabregas and had seemingly pushed the Spaniard's name into the conversation.

However, talk on Fabregas 'did not develop into anything further', according to the publication, with the club ultimately switching their attention to Mauricio Pochettino.

Fabregas has a contract with Como until the summer of 2028, and his future is certainly one to watch given how impressive his team have been.

Pochettino will officially become Man United's fresh head coach on November 18, once his commitments with USA have concluded.

The Argentine's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions will be Sunday's meeting with Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League.

Breaking: England’s potential path to glory proves Nations League is more difficult to win than the World Cup

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes you have to say the unsayable because no one else will.
  • The Nations League is a more difficult competition to win than the World Cup or the European Championships.
  • Though there remain plenty of club football fans who take no interest in international football outside of major tournaments and are sceptical about the Nations League, there has been a noticeable drop in the number of club fans repeating the trite notion it is a pointless competition made up of glorified friendlies no one cares about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes you have to say the unsayable because no one else will.

The Nations League is a more difficult competition to win than the World Cup or the European Championships. Stay with me.

Though there remain plenty of club football fans who take no interest in international football outside of major tournaments and are sceptical about the Nations League, there has been a noticeable drop in the number of club fans repeating the trite notion it is a pointless competition made up of glorified friendlies no one cares about.

My hunch as to why: people are beginning to realise how much of a refreshing addition to the football it really is, plus how many tasty fixtures it produces. And it is that final point — the competition regularly throwing up blockbuster clashes between European heavyweights — that explains why the Nations League might just be the hardest competition to win in international football.

Industry observers note that A disclaimer is needed at this point. The Nations League is not a major tournament like the World Cup or European Championships are. Those competitions take place in single block international breaks during the summer (except when hosted in the Middle East) and the stakes at play mean immeasurably more pressure and psychological challenges as players and teams seek to win the trophies that matter most.

The World Cup and Euros remain more psychologically draining and patently more important. But more difficult to win than the Nations League in a footballing sense? Honestly, no.

Sources indicate that the calibre of opposition is far higher in Europe’s newest event compared with the World Cup or Euros. Just look at Argentina’s route to the World Cup final where they were defeated by Spain.

They faced Algeria, Austria, debutants Jordan, fellow debutants Cape Verde, Egypt, Switzerland and then finally one world-football powerhouse, England, and were suddenly into a World Cup final.

According to recent reports, for all their memories of their best World Cup finish since 1966, England’s route to their semi-final defeat to Argentina was not much more difficult. Croatia, Ghana, Panama, DR Congo, Mexico, and finally Norway.

And in their previous tournament, when England limped to the Euro 2024 final under Gareth Southgate with a string of uninspiring performances, they faced Serbia, Denmark, Slovenia, Slovakia, Switzerland and the Netherlands — and navigating that pretty presentable route meant they had qualified for the final and a shot at becoming European champions.

And what made this summer’s expanded World Cup even less likely to produce those significant fixtures was FIFA’s brazenly cynical introduction of Wimbledon-styled protected ranking at its seeding stage.

The world’s four top-ranked nations would be kept apart in different quarters of the draw until the semi-finals providing they each won their groups. Shock: they all did.

Industry observers note that sure enough, for the first time in history the four top ranks made up the men’s World Cup semi-finalists: Argentina, England, France and Spain. A great product, just as FIFA wanted, but it had taken 100 matches to get there, the only blockbuster fixture among 72 group matches having been Spain and Uruguay, two former winners.

Discover a hidden island paradise in the Indian Ocean.

The World Cup was great, but plenty of its matches had been rather too easy to call beforehand.

The calibre of opposition is far higher in Europe’s newest event compared with the World Cup or Euros.

Now consider England’s potential path to Nations League glory next summer. A group stage first of all where England faced Czechia, Croatia and world champions Spain home and away.

Croatia are a good footballing nation but by finishing third of the group are now out, with next March to bring together only the winners and runners up from the four groups for the quarter-finals.

Group A3 winners England will face either Belgium, the Netherlands or Erling Haaland’s Norway — the teams ranked eighth, ninth and 19th in the world rankings.

After a two-legged tie against one of those opponents, England would gear up for next summer’s Nations League Finals, a one-off semi-final and then potentially a final, with France, Germany or Portugal as their likeliest opponents in those two games.

Here is a string of prestige fixtures far more testing for Thomas Tuchel’s side than the World Cup produced. No comparison in pressure and scrutiny, granted, but tougher in purely footballing terms, undoubtedly — and coaches are not rotating their teams or resting players as much as one might imagine. It is taken seriously.

Sources indicate that for its sheer hit rate of big games out of the total set of fixtures and for how consistently well a top team would have to perform to navigate them all, the UEFA Nations League has become international football’s most difficult competition to win. There. Sometimes you have to say the unsayable because no one else will.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER.

Published: 21:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 17:17 EST, 13 November 2026.

Of 252 clubs in the top seven tiers of English football, the last one unbeaten can be found in the pristine confines of Meadow Park, yards from the studios where the Indiana Jones adventures were filmed.

In a recent development, boreham Wood are on their own crusade. And the Holy Grail is a long-coveted place in the EFL for the runaway leaders of the National League. They have 44 points from 16 games with 44 goals and are 12 points clear ahead of a trip to Yeovil on Saturday, finding success with a distinct passing style.

In a remarkable 4-3 comeback win against Hartlepool earlier this month, Luke Garrard's team made 1,022 passes, beating the Premier League record of 1,015 set by Manchester City against Swansea in April 2018.

The electric start to this campaign is, according to Garrard, fuelled by the lingering pain of defeat in the play-off final at Wembley in May when they conceded an equaliser in the seventh minute of stoppage time and lost on penalties.

Recent findings suggest that 'That broke me mentally for four or five days,' the Wood boss tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I reflected hugely and had a long, hard look at myself because I could not walk back for the first day of pre-season without the energy and heart for the job.

Recent findings suggest that 'I spoke to the owners and the staff about the first meeting I wanted to have when we came back in. It involved everyone at the club, and it was a message to tell all of them that as much as it hurt us, we needed to use the hurt as our fuel and our driving force.

'We got quite lucky getting some results on the board quite rapidly and that builds momentum and belief.'.

National League leaders Boreham Wood, under the guidance of their manager Luke Garrard, are the last unbeaten team in the top seven tiers of English football.

It has been revealed that boreham Wood are a slick operation, skilfully run despite crowds seldom breaking 1,500. They share Meadow Park with Arsenal Women and Arsenal Under 21s and U18s.

Industry observers note that boreham Wood are a slick operation, skilfully run despite crowds seldom breaking 1,500 by chairman Danny Hunter and his son Charlie, who is the sporting director and in charge of recruitment strategy. They are punching above their weight with a mid-table budget.

Hunter senior is a former props master in the film industry who worked at the nearby Elstree Studios among others, and whose father Mickey was a double promotion winning manager of club in the 1970s.

He took control in 1999 and has overseen investment of more than £14million and the rise from the depths of the Isthmian League to the brink of the EFL, forging effective relationships with local authorities and Premier League neighbours Arsenal, who use Meadow Park for their Women, Under-21 and Under-18 teams.

Arsenal ad boards surround an immaculate pitch, and work is underway at the venue on a £4m project to create a covered South Stand terrace incorporating improved 'Fan Zone' style facilities for away fans and a latest first-team building.

Garrard's team train in the mornings on the artificial pitches beside the stadium, which are available for community use in the evenings and home in the afternoons to the club's academy.

According to recent reports, manchester City's Iliman Ndiaye and Hull's Sorba Thomas were both nurtured as young players at Boreham Wood. So was Abdul Abdulmalik, a 23-year-old winger signed after his release from Millwall in 2024 and sold to Djurgardens in Sweden for £1.5m in August.

The Abdulmalik fee shattered the non-League record set when Fleetwood Town sold Jamie Vardy to Leicester in 2012.

There was an untidy episode towards the end of the transfer window when Abdulmalik went public to plead for a move, but the Hunters secured an enviable price for their star and in another example of their good housekeeping have yet to reinvest the money in the team. It is still there as a war chest as they target promotion.

Abdul Abdulmalik, a 23-year-old winger signed after his release from Millwall in 2024, was sold to Djurgardens in Sweden for £1.5million in August.

It has been revealed that the club is run by chairman Danny Hunter (pictured) and his son Charlie, who is the sporting director. Hunter Snr is a former props master in the film industry.

The windfall from Wood's famous FA Cup run in 2021-22 was invested into refitting the interiors of the ground including the dressing rooms and swish hospitality areas recognised among the best in non-League.

Meadow Park has a bar bedecked with souvenirs from those games and named in honour of Mark Ricketts, scorer of the goal to beat Bournemouth, who were at the time bound for promotion to the Premier League, and which clinched a date with Everton in the fifth round at Goodison Park.

According to recent reports, 'At no stage has the chairman given me any pressure to generate money from prize funds and cup runs,' says 41-year-old Garrard. 'It's only ever been about creating moments and memories.

In a recent development, 'He (Hunter) is a Boreham Wood boy through and through and it's always been his greatest wish to lead the club into the EFL. He wants to leave a legacy. I adore him, I think he's a genius. We have a great working relationship. I do not take for granted the luxury of being manager here, especially after losing my job two years ago.'.

Sources indicate that garrard has a long association with the club. First as a player, briefly in 2005 and then returning for a second spell four years later, a loan move from Wimbledon which became permanent and led him into his first coaching roles and the manager's job.

He took control in 2015 with the Wood in the top tier of non-League for the first time. Three times they reached the play-offs without promotion and there were many highs including Goodison before Garrard's tearful exit after relegation in April 2024, only for him to be back in charge by September.

During five months away, he turned down interest from one club because it took him too far from his family home and received two direct and sobering rejections from National League clubs. Feedback from the first told him he 'wasn't on the list and never would be' and from the second that he 'wasn't good enough' for them.

Perhaps it reveals some of football's inherent petty-mindedness towards Boreham Wood. They are perceived by some as upstarts with limited history and small crowds, putting the noses of 'bigger' clubs out of joint with the streamlined success of their business model and Hunter's backing, like a non-League version of Bournemouth or Brentford.

They have been known to charge scouts for tickets and charge away teams to broadcast, which some refuse to do on a point of principle. For a time, they had a reputation for pragmatic and unattractive football – but not any longer.

Garrard was rejected by two National League clubs and found himself back at Boreham Wood. 'The stars aligned,' as he puts it.

Prolific striker Matt Rush has is fuelling Boreham Wood's promotion push.

Sources indicate that garrard was probably entitled to have expected more interest in his services. Instead, he spent two days following the second of those rejections in earnest conversation with his wife about the need to look for work away from football when out of the blue came a call from Boreham Wood.

Within another two days he was back in his old job. 'The stars aligned,' as he puts it. 'It was the best team in the National South with the best players, the best facilities and the best budget. I had to go and deliver.'.

According to recent reports, and he did. With promotion back to the National League at the first attempt. Then the near-miss heartache of Wembley. Now this early-season surge thanks in part to the goals of striker Matt Rush. The Wood seem to have emerged stronger despite selling their most talented individual, which is a reassuring situation for any coach.

Unbeaten since April in the National League, they scored 25 goals in seven games in October and League One Wigan became the first team to beat them in any competition this season, in the FA Cup first round on Saturday.

It could yet prove a blessing in Boreham Wood's quest for the Holy Grail.

#25686. Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures.
  • It has been revealed that the founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227.
  • The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, claims Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

It has been revealed that the founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols.".

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, claims Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?".

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff notes.

Sources indicate that genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, concern legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica.".

It has been revealed that but "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched.".

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

It has been revealed that "In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," notes Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," indicates Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today.".

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.
